title: Stacks and Queues: LIFO and FIFO
learningObjectives: Describe stack behavior as last-in, first-out (LIFO).
Describe queue behavior as first-in, first-out (FIFO).
Explain push, pop, peek, enqueue, and dequeue operations.
Choose a stack or queue based on processing order.
Handle empty structures and capacity or boundary cases.

understand.concept: A stack removes the newest item first (LIFO). A queue removes the oldest item first (FIFO). They may be implemented with arrays, lists, linked structures, or built-in collections; syntax and performance vary.
understand.whyItMatters: Stacks suit undo and backtracking. Queues suit waiting requests and arrival-order processing. Choosing the wrong order can make behavior incorrect.
understand.analogy: A stack of trays: take the top tray first. A service queue: the person at the front is served first.
understand.analogyLimit: Implementations can have capacity, performance, or concurrency limits; a priority queue is not necessarily FIFO.

explain.narrative: Stacks commonly use push, pop, and peek/top. Queues commonly use enqueue, dequeue, and peek/front. Peek inspects without removing. Define empty behavior and capacity handling. For large queues, repeatedly removing the first element of an array may be costly; consider a purpose-built queue.

examples.title: Stack: undo latest action
examples.explanation: Pop removes the newest item, matching LIFO.

examples.title: Stack: inspect top
examples.explanation: Inspection does not remove the item.

examples.title: Queue: serve in arrival order
examples.explanation: The oldest request leaves first, demonstrating FIFO.

examples.title: Queue: inspect front
examples.explanation: The front is next to be dequeued; reading it does not remove it.

examples.title: Compare removal order
examples.explanation: Stack takes newest, queue takes oldest.

commonMistakes: Removing from the wrong end of a queue.
Calling pop or dequeue on an empty structure without defining behavior.
Using array shifting repeatedly for large queues without considering performance.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Trace both structures
guidedTask.instructions: Trace each operation and record contents after it.
steps: Push red, blue, green onto a stack.
Peek and state whether contents change.
Pop twice and record the removal order.
Enqueue red, blue, green into a queue.
Peek at the front and state whether contents change.
Dequeue twice and compare the order with the stack.
guidedTask.starterCode: // Stack: push red, blue, green; peek; pop; pop\n// Queue: enqueue red, blue, green; peek; dequeue; dequeue

independentTask.title: Independent: Order-sensitive design
independentTask.instructions: Create a scenario where order matters and select the correct structure.
requirements: Choose stack or queue and justify LIFO or FIFO.
Add at least four items and show two removals.
Include peek/front and explain whether it changes the structure.
Explain handling of an empty-structure edge case.

hints: Ask whether newest or oldest should leave first.
LIFO: last added, first removed; FIFO: first added, first removed.
Push/pop commonly belong to stacks; enqueue/dequeue to queues.
Sketch the stack or queue while tracing.
Test empty operations and capacity limits.

questions.prompt: A stack receives A, B, C in that order. Which item does pop remove next?
questions.explanation: LIFO removes the newest item first.

questions.prompt: A FIFO queue receives A, B, C. Which item is removed first?
questions.explanation: FIFO removes the oldest waiting item.
Peek/front observes the next item but leaves the structure unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which is a natural stack use?
questions.explanation: Undo commonly reverses the most recent action, matching LIFO.

questions.prompt: Before pop or dequeue, what should robust code consider?
questions.explanation: Empty operations may be invalid or return/throw different outcomes depending on the API.
